segments.source: Terrain energy costs per segment: {'plain': 1, 'forest': 2, 'hill': 3, 'marsh': 4}. Three routes from Iris to Linden: R1=['plain', 'hill', 'plain']; R2=['plain', 'forest', 'plain', 'plain']; R3=['plain', 'marsh']. The traveler can spend at most 8 energy units.
The energy of a route is the sum of its terrain costs. A route above the energy limit is infeasible. Among feasible routes, minimize energy.
Which route is feasible and uses the least energy?
1. Compute route totals: R1=5, R2=5, R3=5. 2. Discard any total above 8. 3. The smallest remaining total is R1=5.
Relief changes the cost of movement; “shortest” and “easiest” are not automatically the same.
Weighted paths with a feasibility budget; sum costs and choose the minimum feasible path.

Problem 36. Classifying climate data: Station A
Climate descriptions summarize long-term patterns. In a reasoning problem, explicit thresholds let us classify numerical data without hidden knowledge.

Use this classroom classification: cool if mean temperature <12°C; mild if 12–17°C; warm if >17°C. Dry if annual precipitation <500 mm; wet if ≥500 mm. Data: Station A: T=8°C, P=430 mm; Station B: T=16°C, P=720 mm; Station C: T=12°C, P=520 mm.
Apply only the stated thresholds. Temperature and precipitation are separate dimensions, so each station receives two labels.
Classify Station A. Then identify whether any other station has the same two-label class.
1. Compare T=8 with the temperature thresholds: it is cool. 2. Compare P=430 with 500 mm: it is dry. 3. Compare the combined label with the other stations; matches: none.
Station A is cool and dry; no other station has the same class.
Classification is the application of clear predicates to data; the rule must be stated before the label is inferred.
Numeric predicates with thresholds; output the conjunction of the temperature and precipitation categories.
